question: According to official sources1, opera singer Ildar Abdrazakov will star in Don Giovanni at the Teatro Filarmonico in Verona in January 2026. Abdrazakov is known for openly supporting the Russian Government and many reports indicate that he is a leading Kremlin propagandist.

He supported the ‘Putin list’ in Russia’s presidential election, speaking publicly in support of the Kremlin’s policies, and Putin rewarded him by appointing him a member of the Presidential Council for Arts and Culture, replacing members who had advocated for peace. Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation has included him in its list of ‘warmongers’, i.e.

staunch proponents of the war, on account of his active support for the Kremlin regime. As a result of his activism and clear political resolve, Abdrazakov has already been banned from some of Europe’s leading stages – with concerts cancelled in Paris, Zurich, Vienna and Rome – and from major theatres in the US. In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware that Abdrazakov is due to perform at the Teatro Filarmonico in Verona?
What measures can – and will – it take to ensure that his appearance is cancelled, taking into account the numerous Russian sanctions packages?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.1.2026) As a consequence of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine the EU does not engage with Russian public entities, including in the field of culture. Russian cultural figures under EU sanctions are subject to an EU entry ban and to the freezing of assets in the EU due to actions undermining Ukraine’s territorial integrity.

The opera singer in question has not been put under the EU’s restrictive measures. Press reports indicate that the performance at the Teatro Filarmonico in Verona in January 2026 has been cancelled. Entry bans can be entered in the Schengen Information System (SIS) based on restrictive measures or a judicial or administrative decision by a Member State.

The Commission has no access to the data in the SIS and therefore cannot establish whether there is an alert on a person for refusal of entry and stay. Russian authorities instrumentalise culture, which in the case of state-controlled cultural and artistic bodies and entities becomes an extended arm of the regime’s propaganda.

It is for Member States, however, to determine the level of cultural cooperation while ensuring that their national policies conform to the Union’s positions as set out in Article 29 of the Treaty on European Union1 and within the existing EU policies vis-à-vis Russia.
